subject: using daply to create array with no values on diagonal

messages.author: 3b469b246ecd3a5b
messages.subject: using daply to create array with no values on diagonal
parts:
I have some data for which there is no data on the diagonal. In
baseball, an example would be the number of times when team A plays
team B (i.e. team A never plays team A). [I didn't see an easy way to
construct my example from the baseball dataset.]

Here is a simple data frame with data that has the logical form of a
3x3 array with no data on the diagonal. I am trying to use daply to
turn this into a 3 x 3 array but haven't succeeded. I this simply a
wrong approach to plyr? daply knows the resulting data has a
structure of 3 x 3, but it doesn't notice that there's no data on the
diagonal.

# create test data: data frame but has pattern of 3 x 3 array
# with no values on the diagonal.
x <- NULL
for(i in 1:3) for(j in 1:3) if(i != j) for(k in 1:4) {
x <- rbind(x, data.frame(i = i, j = j, v = rnorm(1)) )
}

# array is not what I hoped for
daply(x, .(i, j), sum)

#result:
#> daply(x, .(i, j), sum)
# j
#i 2 3 1
# 1 10.375480 19.86966 NA
# 2 15.250084 15.94989 NA
# 3 8.997385 18.25632 NA


# this doesn't help:
daply(x, .(factor(i), factor(j)), sum)

# what I want:
result <- array(NA, dim = c(3,3))
for(i in 1:3) for(j in 1:3) if(i != j){
result[i,j] <- sum(x$v[(x$i == i) & (x$j == j)])
}

#> result
# [,1] [,2] [,3]
#[1,] NA -1.7802108 0.2300103
#[2,] -0.2351738 NA -3.6175024
#[3,] 0.3816883 0.9467433 NA
#[3,] -0.05011412 -1.743681 NA

messages.author: 9e1d805a26f6d719
messages.subject: Re: using daply to create array with no values on diagonal
parts:
This works for me:
daply(x, .(i, j), function(q) sum(q$v))

daply() repeatedly gives part of the df to the function defined in the
third argument. In your case, the third argument was sum(), so it sums
all all values in a slice of the df (including the i and j columns!),
and gives you the wrong answer. You want to sum up just the values in
the v column, so you have to explicitly define a function that takes a
df and returns a scalar.

-Harlan

Hi:

Here's another way to go about it. Given your input data frame x,

s <- ddply(x, .(i, j), summarise, v1 = sum(v))
m <- matrix(NA, 3, 3)
m[cbind(s$i, s$j)] <- s$v1
> m
           [,1]      [,2]       [,3]
[1,]         NA 0.2568042  0.1201668
[2,] -1.5188118        NA -3.5773508
[3,]  0.6867254 0.1402535         NA

This illustrates the use of a two-column index matrix to assign values to the target matrix. More below.

I have to mention that this is NOT the way to input data in R. The bigger the matrix/data frame you want to create, the progressively slower this approach will become. This is closer to the 'R way':

x <- data.frame(i = rep(1:3, each = 12), j = rep(rep(1:3, each = 4), 3), v = rnorm(36))
x <- subset(x, i != j)

The use of rbind() to add one row at a time is definitely not recommended, as it forces recursive copying of the data frame/matrix in RAM. The bigger the end object becomes, the more memory gets eaten with all of the copies of the input object. Using vectorization whenever possible is far more memory efficient and usually faster. This is a common problem with folks who move from programming languages like Fortran, C or Java to R.

How much difference does it make? Let's test it:

 f <- function() {   
      x <- data.frame(i = rep(1:3, each = 12), j = rep(rep(1:3, each = 4), 3), v = rnorm(36))
      subset(x, i != j)
   }
g <- function() {

x <- NULL
      for(i in 1:3) for(j in 1:3) if(i != j) for(k in 1:4) {
         x <- rbind(x, data.frame(i = i, j = j, v = rnorm(1)) )   }
  }

# Run both functions 1000 times and note the cumulative time:
> system.time(replicate(1000, f()))
   user  system elapsed
    0.9     0.0     0.9
> system.time(replicate(1000, g()) )
   user  system elapsed
  26.70    0.04   26.73

We can write a function to do the entire thing:

offdiag <- function() {
   x <- data.frame(i = rep(1:3, each = 12), j = rep(rep(1:3, each = 4), 3), v = rnorm(36))
   x <- subset(x, i != j)
   s <- ddply(x, .(i, j), summarise, v1 = sum(v))
   m <- matrix(NA, 3, 3)
   m[cbind(s$i, s$j)] <- s$v1
   m
   }
> offdiag()
          [,1]       [,2]       [,3]
[1,]        NA -0.7289988  4.2572501
[2,]  1.433711         NA -0.9659355
[3,] -3.108911  3.1496482         NA
> system.time(replicate(1000, offdiag()))
   user  system elapsed
   7.66    0.00    7.68

This function, which creates the data, does the summation and reshapes it into a matrix, is almost four times faster than your function to read in the data. This shows you that the use of vectorized functions is usually a better way to go in R, although there are occasions where adept use of looping can be faster.

Be aware that I'm not trying to dump on you - this is actually an important lesson that needs to be learned in order to operate efficiently in R. The use of matrix indexing is another useful trick worth remembering.

As an exercise, here's my attempt to make a test case using Dennis's
code. I also included my original loop code so that it provides a
test that does not involve plyr in both arguments of the all.equal.

x <- subset(data.frame(i = rep(1:3, each = 12), j = rep(rep(1:3, each
= 4), 3), v = seq(1:36)), i != j)
y <- daply(x, .(i, j), function(q) sum(q$v))

s <- ddply(x, .(i, j), summarise, v1 = sum(v))
m <- matrix(NA, 3, 3)
m[cbind(s$i, s$j)] <- s$v1

result_loop <- array(NA, dim = c(3,3))
for(i in 1:3) for(j in 1:3) if(i != j){

result_loop[i,j] <- sum(x$v[(x$i == i) & (x$j == j)])
}

all.equal(m, y)
all.equal(m, result_loop)
all.equal(y, result_loop)

Of course the trick is that for now at least you would not want to
rely on a test case that I wrote!
--John
